To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the optimization of cancer therapy requires the identification and formalization of the optimum level of treatment effect, that the optimum level of cancer treatment effect is a range of levels, and that the optimum level is a function of the patient's age, sex, and disease state.

the optimum dose of radiation for cancer treatment is a function of the tumor type, the tumor site, the patient's age, sex, and general health, and the treatment method, and that the optimum dose is the dose that maximizes the benefit to risk ratio for that particular tumor, tumor site, and patient.
the optimum dose-response curve is the one that has the greatest slope at a given point on the dose axis and that this curve is not necessarily the one that has a steepest slope at a given dose.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the methodology and the generation of the information necessary for the optimization of radiation therapy.
the development of a method for the optimization of treatment in the individual patient.
a systematic approach to the identification and formalization of the optimum level of benefit and risk in the treatment of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimum cancer treatment is the one that produces a net benefit to the patient and that this is not a decision to be made in advance of the treatment.
optimization is the process of identifying and formalizing the optimum level of response in the treatment selected.
, in the absence of a comprehensive and detailed conclusion, the best practice, individualised treatment method is the optimum method for the optimization of radiotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are attempting to define the optimum level of treatment effect and to identify it in the individual patient.
optimization of cancer treatment is possible and that it is a necessary part of the development of the science and art of cancer treatment.
we are attempting to define a new clinical research methodology for cancer treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the clinical trial is not a method for the identification of optimum cancer treatment, and that, if optimum treatment is to be identified and formalized, it must be done by the best practice, individual treatment method.
the clinical trial, as currently structured, does not lend itself to the identification of optimum levels of effect in cancer treatment.
the best treatment for any given patient is not necessarily the one that gives the most benefit and the least risk.
